newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Saudis said pushing hard for quick WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: Saudis said pushing hard for quick WTO entry.

text.p: Saudi Arabia, pushing hard for quick entry to the World Trade Organisation, pledged on Wednesday to bend every effort to satisfy trading partners it was committed to observe the body's rules, diplomats said.

According to trade envoys, the promise was made at a meeting of a working party studying the Saudi application to join the WTO -- which currently has 125 members, including most Arab states in the Gulf.

They said Riyadh's Commerce Minister Osamah bin Jaafar bin Ibrahim Faqih told the meeting his country recognised that early admission to the body -- watchdog over most global trade -- would require "energetic efforts" from all sides.
"The Saudis are evidently intent on moving quickly," said one source.

Faqih came to Geneva with a 40-member delegation for the talks, the second round of entry negotiations for the oil giant and for bilateral talks with individual countries on tariff schedules for goods and services.

Wednesday's meeting, attended by envoys from many members of the WTO, focused on intellectual property rights including patents and copyright protection and on trade-related investments measures, trade sources said.
The Saudi minister told the working group his government was making a major effort to adapt to the WTO's standards and norms for intellectual property protection, according to the sources.
But he said Riyadh, with a lack of know-how in this area and need for training for officials, would need some flexibility in the timing for implementing all the body's rules.

Diplomats said a United States official praised Saudi Arabia for having a good record on intellectual property protection. The European Union, which has welcomed the application, said it would be looking for more detailed information in some areas.
Saudi Arabia is seeking WTO membership as a developing country, which would give it a special transition period to bring its legislation and practices into line with the rules.

It originally applied to join the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the WTO's predcecessor, in 1993 but a working party set up then made no progress. The first meeting of the WTO group was held in May this year.

On Thursday, the Saudi delegation is due to hold separate talks with the United States, the EU, Canada, Japan and Switzerland, and on Friday the working party will meet again to look at the goods and services sector.

Under working party procedure, an applicant country submits an initial report on its trade policies and WTO members then come back with detailed questions. Sometimes this process can take many months or even years.
China has been negotiating entry to GATT, and now the WTO, for almost a decade, but progress has been generally held up over political issues. Russia is moving towards the third year of the process.
Other Middle Eastern countries among the 31 around the world who have applications under study are Oman and Jordan. Israel, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates are already members.
But Western states have blocked a bid from Iran to start the process.
